CausalChain: Dietary polyphenols -> Reduce hepatic oxidative stress -> Enhance hepatic PPARβ/δ activity -> Upregulate lipogenic genes -> Increase synthesis of PC (18:0/18:1) -> Circulation and targeted delivery to muscle (confirmed via stable isotope tracing) -> Activation of muscle PPARα -> Enhanced muscle fatty acid uptake and oxidation -> Decreased circulating triglycerides and lipid overload
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that dietary supplementation with polyphenol-rich extracts, by reducing hepatic oxidative stress, specifically enhances hepatic PPARβ/δ activity. This activation upregulates a set of lipogenic genes responsible for increasing the synthesis of the specific phosphatidylcholine, PC (18:0/18:1). Utilizing modern stable isotope lipidomics and wearable biosensors to monitor real-time metabolite fluxes, we propose that the PC (18:0/18:1) is secreted into the circulation and efficiently delivered to skeletal muscle. Once in muscle tissue, PC (18:0/18:1) either alone or in synergy with endogenous lipid mediators, activates PPARα, thereby promoting fatty acid uptake and oxidation. The resulting metabolic shift contributes to lowered circulating triglycerides and alleviates both dyslipidemia and hepatic steatosis. Moreover, CRISPR-Cas9 mediated gene-editing will be employed to specifically perturb hepatic PPARβ/δ and muscle PPARα functions, providing mechanistic insights and validation of each sequential step in this cascade.
Abstract: In this study, we propose an integrative hypothesis that leverages contemporary metabolomic and gene-editing technologies to elucidate a novel liver‐to‐muscle signaling mechanism mediating the metabolic benefits of dietary polyphenols. Specifically, dietary polyphenol supplementation reduces hepatic oxidative stress, which potentiates hepatic PPARβ/δ activity, triggering the upregulation of lipogenic genes that favor the synthesis of the specific phosphatidylcholine species PC (18:0/18:1). Advanced stable isotope tracing and high‐throughput lipidomics are used to verify the secretion and transport of PC (18:0/18:1) to skeletal muscle, where its interaction, together with other endogenous ligands, activates muscle PPARα. This receptor activation enhances muscle fatty acid uptake and oxidation, resulting in decreased circulating triglycerides and mitigating lipid overload. CRISPR-Cas9 gene modulation further allows the dissection of the specific roles of hepatic PPARβ/δ and muscle PPARα in this metabolic cascade, thus strengthening the causal framework of interorgan lipid signaling in metabolic homeostasis.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis suggested that polyphenol-rich extracts enhance hepatic PPARβ/δ activity to upregulate PC (18:0/18:1) production, which in turn activates muscle PPARα to promote fatty acid oxidation and improve metabolic parameters. In the revised hypothesis, we retained the core causal chain but enhanced its plausibility and specificity by: 1) incorporating the reduction of hepatic oxidative stress as an initiating event that facilitates PPARβ/δ activation; 2) emphasizing the use of advanced technologies such as stable isotope tracing, high-throughput lipidomics, and wearable biosensors to track the production, circulation, and tissue-specific delivery of PC (18:0/18:1); 3) integrating CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing tools to provide targeted functional validation of both hepatic and muscle PPAR pathways; and 4) clearly delineating the cascade from hepatic modulation to muscle receptor activation, thereby strengthening the mechanistic links and practical implementability of the hypothesis.
